title: The Rise of Rome | From Village to Empire (753 BC - AD 117)
description: How a village of huts on the Tiber became the largest empire of the ancient western world: kings, Republic, Carthage and Hannibal, Caesar, Augustus, and Trajan's high-water mark in AD 117.
text: Rome, the eighth century BC. On a hill above a marshy bend of the river Tiber, a few hundred farmers and shepherds live in huts of timber, reeds and clay. Their neighbours are older, richer and far stronger. Nine hundred years later, the descendants of those villagers rule from the hills of northern Britain to the shores of the Persian Gulf: perhaps sixty million people, one in five of all the humans alive. The Greek historian Polybius, who watched Rome's rise as a hostage in the city, put the question bluntly. Who is so worthless or so idle, he wrote, as not to wish to know how, and under what kind of government, the Romans in less than fifty three years brought nearly the whole inhabited world under their rule? Fifty three years was only the beginning. This is the story of how a village became an empire. Chapter one. The wolf's city. The Romans told their own beginning as a legend. Twin boys, Romulus and Remus, sons of the war god Mars, were cast into the Tiber, suckled by a she wolf and raised by a shepherd. Grown to manhood, they founded a city on the Palatine Hill, quarrelled over its walls, and Romulus killed his brother. Livy, writing under Augustus, admits that such tales are more fit for poets than for reliable history. The traditional date, the twenty first of April, seven hundred and fifty three BC, was calculated centuries later by the scholar Varro. Archaeology tells a quieter story. On the Palatine, excavators have found the post holes of Iron Age huts from the eighth century BC, and traces of an early wall, though its date is still argued. Rome grew where a river crossing met the salt road, between the Etruscan cities to the north and the Latins and Greeks to the south. In the Forum, beneath a pavement of black stone, archaeologists found one of the oldest Latin inscriptions known, a sixth century sacred law that names a king. Tradition gives Rome seven kings. The last three were Etruscans, and under them the marsh was drained and the Forum laid out. From the Etruscans, too, came the fasces, the bundle of rods and an axe carried before every Roman magistrate as the sign of his power. The last of all, Tarquin the Proud, was remembered as a tyrant. According to Livy, when his son raped the noblewoman Lucretia and she took her own life, the nobles rose, and in five hundred and nine BC they drove the king out. The Romans swore never again to be ruled by a king. Power passed to two consuls, elected each year, and to a council of elders, the Senate. For centuries its motto would be carried on the standards: the Senate and the People of Rome. Chapter two. Masters of Italy. The young Republic fought its neighbours almost every summer. Its greatest rival was Veii, a rich Etruscan city just sixteen kilometres up the Tiber. Livy says the Romans besieged it for ten years, until the general Camillus took it in three hundred and ninety six BC, by a tunnel dug beneath the walls. Rome doubled its land at a stroke. Then catastrophe came from the north. Gallic warriors crossed the Apennines, destroyed a Roman army at the river Allia, and sacked Rome itself, in three hundred and ninety BC by the Roman count, or perhaps three hundred and eighty seven. Only the Capitol held out; Livy tells how the sacred geese of Juno woke the defenders when the Gauls tried to climb it by night. When the Romans paid a ransom in gold and complained that the scales were rigged, the Gallic chief Brennus, says Livy, threw his sword onto the weights and spoke two words: vae victis, woe to the conquered. Rome never forgot it. The city rebuilt, raised a stone wall, and turned south. In three hundred and twelve BC the censor Appius Claudius began the first great Roman road, the Appian Way, to carry the legions south. In three long wars against the Samnites of the central mountains, Rome suffered humiliation at the Caudine Forks, where a whole army was forced to pass beneath a yoke of spears, and won victory at Sentinum, in two hundred and ninety five BC. Its secret weapon was not the sword but the treaty: defeated peoples became allies, kept their own towns, and sent soldiers to Rome's wars. In two hundred and eighty BC the Greek city of Tarentum called in Pyrrhus, King of Epirus, a cousin of Alexander the Great, with elephants and a professional phalanx. Pyrrhus beat the Romans at Heraclea and again at Asculum, but at a dreadful cost. Plutarch has him say that one more such victory would utterly ruin him. Beaten at Beneventum in two hundred and seventy five BC, he sailed home. By two hundred and sixty four BC, Rome controlled the whole peninsula, from the river Arno to the toe of Italy. Chapter three. War at sea. Across a strait just three kilometres wide lay Sicily, and beyond it Carthage, a Phoenician trading city in what is now Tunisia, the richest power in the western Mediterranean, with the greatest navy of its age. In two hundred and sixty four BC both powers were drawn into a quarrel over Messana, on the Sicilian strait. It became a war that lasted twenty three years. Rome had almost no warships. Polybius says the Romans used a stranded Carthaginian galley as their model and built a fleet of one hundred quinqueremes and twenty triremes, training their rowers on benches on dry land. They added a weapon of their own, a boarding bridge with an iron spike that the soldiers called the raven. In two hundred and sixty BC, off Mylae on the north coast of Sicily, the consul Gaius Duilius met the Carthaginian fleet. The ravens dropped, the legionaries charged across, and the sea battle became a land battle. An inscription from his victory column, still in Rome, boasts of thirty one ships captured and thirteen sunk. In two hundred and fifty six BC a Roman army even landed in Africa, only to be destroyed outside Carthage by a Spartan mercenary general. The war ground on through storms that drowned whole Roman fleets, until in two hundred and forty one BC a new fleet destroyed the Carthaginians off the Aegates Islands. Carthage gave up Sicily, Rome's first overseas province, and soon Sardinia and Corsica followed. In time the Romans would call the Mediterranean simply our sea. Chapter four. Hannibal. Carthage rebuilt its power in Spain, under the Barca family. The general Hamilcar, it was said, made his nine year old son swear at an altar never to be a friend of Rome. That son was Hannibal. In two hundred and eighteen BC, after he took the Roman ally Saguntum, war came again, and Hannibal did what no one expected. He marched from New Carthage, through the Pyrenees and southern Gaul, across the Rhone, and over the Alps in late autumn, with war elephants. Polybius says the army left Spain with ninety thousand foot and twelve thousand horse, but only about twenty thousand infantry and six thousand cavalry reached the plains of Italy. Exactly which pass he crossed is still debated. What followed was a nightmare for Rome. In December, at the river Trebia, Hannibal ambushed a consular army in the snow. In June of the following year, at Lake Trasimene, he hid his army in the morning mist and trapped another; some fifteen thousand Romans died, among them the consul. Then, on the second of August two hundred and sixteen BC, at Cannae in Apulia, the Romans brought the largest army they had ever fielded, perhaps eighty six thousand men. Hannibal let his centre bend back, closed his African infantry on both flanks, and sent his cavalry into their rear. The Romans were surrounded. Polybius puts the dead at seventy thousand; Livy, at about fifty thousand. Either way, it was one of the bloodiest single days in the history of war. Livy says Hannibal's brother later poured a heap of gold rings, taken from dead Roman knights, onto the floor of the Carthaginian senate. Yet Hannibal did not march on Rome. His cavalry commander Maharbal is said to have told him: you know how to win a victory, Hannibal, but not how to use one. Yet Rome would not make peace. It refused even to ransom its prisoners. It fought a war of delay in Italy, led by Quintus Fabius Maximus, nicknamed the Delayer, and carried the war abroad. In two hundred and seven BC Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal crossed the Alps with a second army and was destroyed at the river Metaurus; Livy says his head was thrown into Hannibal's camp. A young general, Publius Cornelius Scipio, captured New Carthage, drove the Carthaginians from Spain, and in two hundred and four BC landed in Africa. Hannibal was recalled to defend his city. At Zama, in two hundred and two BC, Hannibal's elephants charged down lanes that Scipio had left open in his lines, and Rome's Numidian allies broke the Carthaginian cavalry. Hannibal had lost his first great pitched battle. Carthage surrendered its fleet and its empire, and Scipio came home with a new name: Africanus. Chapter five. Mistress of the Mediterranean. Rome turned east, to the kingdoms carved from Alexander's empire. In one hundred and ninety seven BC, at Cynoscephalae, the legions broke the Macedonian phalanx of King Philip the Fifth. In one hundred and ninety, at Magnesia in Asia Minor, they routed the Seleucid king Antiochus the Great. And at Pydna, in one hundred and sixty eight, the consul Aemilius Paullus destroyed the army of the last king of Macedon, Perseus. Polybius, the Greek hostage, saw it from the inside and explained it to his readers: the legion's flexible maniples could fight anywhere, while the phalanx was unbeatable only on flat, open ground. Then Rome finished its old enemy. The elder Cato, it was said, ended every speech in the Senate with the same words: Carthage must be destroyed. In one hundred and forty nine BC Rome found a pretext. After a three year siege, in one hundred and forty six BC, Scipio Aemilianus stormed Carthage. The city burned for days, and the survivors, perhaps fifty thousand, were sold into slavery. Polybius stood beside Scipio and saw him weep, quoting Homer on the fall of Troy and fearing the same fate one day for Rome. The famous story that the Romans sowed the ground with salt is a modern invention. In the same year, Roman troops sacked Corinth in Greece. Africa and Macedonia became provinces. Polybius had his answer: in the fifty three years from the eve of Hannibal's war to the fall of Macedon, Rome had become the master of the known world. From Spain to Asia Minor, the Mediterranean world now answered to the Senate. Chapter six. The Republic turns on itself. Conquest brought slaves and silver by the shipload, and the rich bought up the land of the small farmers who had filled the legions. In one hundred and thirty three BC the tribune Tiberius Gracchus passed a law to give public land back to the poor. Senators and their followers beat him to death with clubs and the legs of benches; Plutarch says more than three hundred of his supporters died with him. It was the first time since the kings that political blood had been shed in the streets. Twelve years later his brother Gaius met the same end, and some three thousand of his followers were killed. Then came the generals. Gaius Marius, a new man from the country, opened the legions to the landless poor, who now looked to their commander, not the state, for land when they retired. Marius was consul seven times, and in one hundred and two and one hundred and one BC he destroyed the migrating Cimbri and Teutones, who had wiped out Roman armies in Gaul. Then Rome's Italian allies, refused citizenship, rose in the Social War. Rome won, and gave them the vote anyway. In eighty eight BC Lucius Cornelius Sulla did the unthinkable: he marched his legions on Rome itself. After a war in the east against Mithridates of Pontus, he returned, made himself dictator, and posted lists of his enemies in the Forum. Anyone named could be killed for a reward. Five years after his death, a gladiator named Spartacus led tens of thousands of slaves across Italy; when the revolt was crushed, Appian says six thousand captives were crucified along the Appian Way. The Republic survived Sulla, but every ambitious man had now seen the road to power. Chapter seven. Pompey and Caesar. The man who first took that road to its end was Gnaeus Pompeius, Pompey the Great. In sixty seven BC he swept the pirates from the Mediterranean in a single summer. Then he conquered the east, ended the Seleucid kingdom, and in sixty three BC took Jerusalem. In sixty BC he joined the richest man in Rome, Crassus, and an ambitious aristocrat deep in debt, Gaius Julius Caesar, in an informal pact. As governor of Gaul from fifty eight BC, Caesar conquered everything between the Rhine and the Atlantic, crossed twice into Britain, and wrote his own account of it all. Plutarch claims that in less than ten years Caesar took eight hundred towns and fought three million men, killing one million and enslaving another million. Ancient numbers like these were meant to impress, and modern historians treat them with caution, but the toll was terrible. In fifty two BC all Gaul rose under the Arvernian chief Vercingetorix. Caesar trapped him in the hill fort of Alesia and built two rings of siege works, one facing in and one facing out, some thirty five kilometres in all, and beat off a relief army said to number a quarter of a million. Excavations around Alesia have found his ditches and traps. Vercingetorix laid down his arms at Caesar's feet. Crassus, hungry for glory of his own, invaded Parthia and died at Carrhae in the deserts of Mesopotamia, where Plutarch says twenty thousand Romans fell. With Crassus gone, the Senate turned to Pompey. Ordered to give up his army, Caesar crossed the little river Rubicon into Italy in January forty nine BC. Suetonius gives his words: the die is cast. At Pharsalus in Greece, on the ninth of August forty eight BC, Caesar defeated Pompey, who fled to Egypt and was murdered as he stepped ashore. Caesar made himself dictator, first for ten years, then for life. On the Ides of March, forty four BC, senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed him to death at a meeting of the Senate. Suetonius counts twenty three wounds. Chapter eight. The last civil war. Caesar's will named his great nephew, the eighteen year old Gaius Octavius, as his son and heir. Octavian joined Caesar's lieutenant Mark Antony, and in forty two BC, at Philippi in Macedonia, they crushed the assassins. Brutus and Cassius both took their own lives. Before that, the new allies had settled their scores at home. Appian says some three hundred senators were listed for death, and the orator Cicero, the Republic's loudest voice, was hunted down; his head and hands were nailed to the speakers' platform in the Forum. The victors divided the Roman world. Antony took the east, and the Queen of Egypt, Cleopatra, last of the Ptolemies, as his ally and lover. Octavian took Italy and the west, and the war of words. On the second of September thirty one BC, off the headland of Actium in western Greece, Octavian's admiral Agrippa trapped the fleet of Antony and Cleopatra. The queen broke out with her squadron and fled, and Antony followed her. Within a year Octavian entered Alexandria. Antony fell on his sword. Cleopatra, rather than be paraded through Rome, died by her own hand, by legend from the bite of an asp. Egypt, the richest land in the Mediterranean, became the private possession of one man. In January twenty seven BC, the Senate gave Octavian a new name: Augustus, the revered one. In his own record, the Res Gestae, set up in bronze outside his tomb, he claimed to have handed the Republic back to the Senate and People. After that time, he wrote, I excelled all in influence, but I had no more power than my colleagues. In truth, the Republic was over. Rome had an emperor. Chapter nine. The Roman peace. Augustus ruled for forty one years. He cut the armies of the civil wars to some twenty eight legions, stationed them on the frontiers, and paid them from a new military treasury. Suetonius says he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble. The doors of the temple of Janus, open whenever Rome was at war, had been shut only twice since the founding of the city; Augustus boasted that under him they were shut three times. The conquests went on, to the Alps and the Danube and northern Spain. But in AD nine, in the Teutoburg Forest of Germany, the general Varus lost three entire legions to the Germanic chief Arminius. Suetonius says the old emperor beat his head against a door, crying: Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions. The Rhine became the frontier, and Augustus advised his heirs to keep the empire within its limits. Mostly, they listened. Claudius invaded Britain in AD forty three. Under the Flavian emperors the Colosseum rose in the heart of Rome, opened in AD eighty with a hundred days of games, the year after Vesuvius buried Pompeii. Then, in AD ninety eight, the throne passed to a soldier from Spain, the first emperor born outside Italy: Trajan. In two hard wars he crossed the Danube and conquered Dacia, the gold rich kingdom of King Decebalus, in what is now Romania. The war is carved in a spiral frieze some two hundred metres long around Trajan's Column, still standing in Rome. In AD one hundred and fourteen he turned on Parthia. He annexed Armenia, took Mesopotamia, captured the Parthian capital Ctesiphon in AD one hundred and sixteen, and sailed down the Tigris to the Persian Gulf. There, says Cassius Dio, he watched a ship leaving for India and said: I should certainly have crossed over to the Indians too, if I were still young. In that moment the Roman Empire reached the greatest extent it would ever know, perhaps five million square kilometres, from northern Britain to the Gulf. But revolts were already burning behind him, in Mesopotamia and among the Jewish communities of the east. In August AD one hundred and seventeen, Trajan died on his way home. His successor, Hadrian, gave up the new eastern provinces almost at once, and in time began building walls. The historian Tacitus, writing in Trajan's reign, put into the mouth of a British chieftain the most famous judgement ever passed on Rome: they make a desert, and call it peace. The village on the Tiber had become the greatest empire the western world had seen. It would never be larger again. How it held on for three more centuries in the west, and a thousand years in the east, is another story.
